units.text: We represent Cedar Workshop in Hyderabad. The client hired a laser cutter and returned it on 12 September 2026. The equipment owner retains the Rs 90,000 deposit, alleging damage to the lens, which the client denies. The owner claims to have an inspection report but has not supplied it to our client. Our client has a signed hire agreement and a bank transfer receipt, neither of which have been supplied or checked here. Separately, the owner's technician holds the client's original design drive, which was lent for setup only. The owner claims it may retain this drive until repair charges are paid.

Regarding the deposit and alleged damage dispute: If the hire agreement includes terms on deposit retention for damage, the owner may be entitled to retain the deposit to cover repair costs. However, the obligation on the owner to provide evidence, such as the inspection report alleging damage, is fundamental. Without this evidence supplied to the client, retention of the deposit could be challenged. The denial of damage by the client and absence of the inspection report weakens the owner's position. The signed hire agreement and bank transfer receipt (once reviewed) will clarify the terms and payments made, vital for assessing the dispute.

Regarding the separate dispute over the original design drive: The owner's technician retaining the client's original design drive lent only for setup raises issues of possession and lien. Retaining client property as security or lien for repair charges generally requires express contractual authorization or clear legal basis. Absent such authorization, the continued holding of the design drive may constitute unlawful withholding. The client may have a right to demand return unless a proper repair charge is established and agreed upon, and the alleged lien is lawful. This situation requires examination of the hire agreement or any ancillary agreements relating to possession of client materials.

Considering the opposing positions presented: The owner alleges damage and produces an inspection report (not supplied), justifying deposit retention, and claims a lien on the design drive pending repair charges payment. The client denies damage, requests the inspection report, and holds original contractual and payment documents. Both disputes hinge on documentary evidence, contractual interpretation, and legality of property retention. Without admitting damage or inventing terms, the analysis highlights evidential and legal gaps favoring a challenge to the owner's retention acts if evidence remains undisclosed or contractually unsupported.

Important questions for our client include: 1) Can the client provide a copy of the signed hire agreement and bank transfer receipt to verify terms and payments? 2) Has the client formally requested the inspection report from the owner, and what is the owner's response? 3) Are there any terms in the hire agreement regarding deposits, damage liabilities, and the requirement for inspection or evidence? 4) Is there express contractual authorization permitting the owner or technician to retain the design drive pending payment of repair charges? 5) What is the client's valuation or evidence regarding the condition of the laser cutter and lens at return? 6) Has the client documented any communications or attempts to retrieve the design drive? These questions will guide further legal strategy.
Per instruction, no party communications are to be initiated, no admission of damage is made, and no agreement terms are created beyond the existing documents presented by the client.
